                                      PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

                                                     §
    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
   LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §
   STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                     §                     OF TEXAS
                                                     §
                                                     §


                             SCHAPER ENERGY CONSULTING LLC

                  RESPONSE TO STAFF DISCUSSION DRAFT 16 TAC §25.194

                                    DATED FEBRUARY 13, 2026


                                          I.​ INTRODUCTION


        Schaper Energy Consulting LLC (“Respondent”) respectfully submits these comments in

response to Staff’s Proposal for Publication of new 16 TAC §25.194, filed as Item No. 107 in Project No.

58481 on February 13, 2026, and scheduled for consideration at the Commission’s February 20, 2026

Open Meeting (Agenda Item No. 27). Respondent is a Houston-based strategic and technical advisory

firm providing interconnection, transmission planning, and regulatory advisory services exclusively to

large load developers in the ERCOT market. Respondent’s clients represent a significant share of the

state’s new industrial and data center load growth.       Respondent has participated actively in this

proceeding from its inception, including filing responses to Staff’s September 12, 2025, questions,

comments on the December 2, 2025, first discussion draft, and the January 2, 2026, second discussion

draft, and participating in the January 2026 stakeholder workshop.


        Respondent supports the Commission’s objective of establishing transparent, predictable, and

efficient interconnection standards that balance system reliability with economic development. However,

three provisions in the Staff’s Proposal for Publication present serious concerns that, if adopted as

proposed, threaten to materially impair large load development in Texas and undermine the economic


                                                                                                      1
 competitiveness that PURA §37.0561(b) was enacted to protect. Respondent addresses these provisions

below: (1) the site control provisions in §25.194(d)(1) and (f)(1), which exclude purchase options entirely

and accept only executed leases or deeds at every stage of the process, (2) the forfeiture of 80% of the

$100,000 per MW financial security posted under §25.194(d)(10) upon withdrawal under

§25.194(g)(3)–(4), at a stage when the customer has received no interconnection study results and knows

nothing about available capacity, required upgrades, costs, or energization timeline; (3) the application of

that forfeited 80% as an offset to the interconnecting TSP’s rate base under §25.194(g)(4) and (h)(4),

which constitutes a direct subsidy from developers to other ratepayers with no cost-causation link, while

simultaneously creating a disincentive for TSPs to pursue cost-effective interconnections..


           II.​ THE EXCLUSION OF PURCHASE OPTIONS IS INCOMPATIBLE WITH

       COMMERCIAL REAL ESTATE DEVELOPMENT AND WILL THREATEN BUSINESS

                                        DEVELOPMENT IN TEXAS


        Staff’s Proposal for Publication requires a large load customer to demonstrate site control at both

the intermediate agreement stage (§25.194(d)(1)) and the interconnection agreement stage (§25.194(f)(1))

through one of only two instruments: (A) a signed and executed lease agreement for a duration of at least

five years from the date the customer is expected to reach contracted peak demand, or (B) a deed.


        Notably absent from both provisions are references to purchase options, contracts for sale, ground

lease options, or any other enforceable legal interest short of an executed lease or fee simple ownership.

The Proposal for Publication thus requires either outright ownership or an executed long-term lease

before the customer may even apply to begin the interconnection process.


        This is a material departure from the statutory language.        PURA §37.0561(g) requires the

standards to include “a method for a large load customer…to demonstrate site control for the proposed

load location through an ownership interest, lease, or another legal interest acceptable to the commission.”



                                                                                                          2
 The Legislature expressly contemplated that legal interests beyond fee simple ownership and leases would

qualify.    By limiting acceptable site control to only a deed or an executed lease, Staff’s proposal

effectively reads the phrase “or another legal interest acceptable to the commission” out of the statute.

This is inconsistent with the statutory directive and with established canons of statutory construction

requiring that every word of a statute be given effect.


           The exclusion of purchase options is fundamentally inconsistent with established commercial real

estate development practices. In the infrastructure development industry, and in data center development

in particular, developers routinely secure site access through purchase option agreements, contracts for

sale, ground leases, or other enforceable legal interests that provide the developer with the right, but not

the obligation, to acquire the property.      This optionality is not a deficiency; it is the standard and

universally accepted mechanism by which developers manage risk in the face of development

uncertainties, including the very interconnection study results that the developer is seeking by applying to

the ERCOT process. A developer that exercises a purchase option pays the landowner consideration for

the exclusive right to acquire the property within a defined period, during which the developer conducts

due diligence, including an interconnection study. If the study results are unfavorable, the developer

declines to exercise the option. If favorable, the developer closes on the property. This is rational,

disciplined development.


           Requiring fee simple ownership or an executed lease before the customer may even apply for an

intermediate agreement forces the developer to make an irrevocable land acquisition commitment before

the developer has received any indication of whether the site is electrically feasible, what transmission

upgrades may be required, what the cost of interconnection may be, or what the timeline for service may

look like. For a typical hyperscale data center site in Texas, land acquisition costs can range from tens to

hundreds of millions of dollars. If the interconnection study subsequently reveals that the site requires

prohibitive transmission upgrades, or that available capacity without upgrades is a fraction of the



                                                                                                          3
 requested load, or that the energization timeline exceeds the developer’s commercial requirements, the

developer has no viable path to recover its land costs. The land acquisition becomes a sunk cost with

limited alternative uses absent the planned project.      No rational developer would accept this risk

allocation voluntarily, and no rational developer needs to accept it, because no other market in the United

States requires it.


        Respondent has raised this concern repeatedly throughout these proceedings, and the issue has

now reached a critical point at which these site control provisions threaten to drive business out of Texas.

The Proposal for Publication is more restrictive than the earlier discussion drafts, which at least accepted

purchase options at the initial application stage before progressively narrowing acceptable instruments at

later stages.   The Proposal for Publication eliminates options entirely at every stage, including the

threshold application. This is the most restrictive site-control standard in any interconnection framework

in the United States. Further, our research suggests that: (1) every ISO that has formal site control

requirements for any interconnection type, generation or load, accepts options or deposits in lieu of site

control; (2) no ISO that is developing load-specific interconnection frameworks has proposed restricting

site control to deed or executed lease only; and (3) ERCOT's own generation interconnection rules under

Planning Guide §5.3.2.1(1)(c)-(d) accept options. The proposed §25.194 would therefore be more

restrictive than any interconnection framework in the country, generation or load, and more restrictive

than ERCOT's existing generation rules.


        If Texas adopts unduly restrictive site-control standards for large load interconnections — at a

time when large-load development is a multi-state, multi-ISO competitive process — the predictable

result is that developers will deploy capital to more accommodating markets. Our clients have stated as

much without equivocation. This outcome would be directly contrary to the stated purpose of PURA

§37.0561(b). Respondent strongly recommends that the Commission revise §25.194(d)(1) and (f)(1) to

accept, at a minimum, the same categories of site control instruments recognized in ERCOT’s generation



                                                                                                          4
 interconnection process: fee simple ownership; a binding contract for sale; a purchase option agreement

supported by consideration; a ground lease or option to enter a ground lease; or any other enforceable

legal interest sufficient to establish the developer’s right to use and develop the site.         At the

interconnection agreement stage, if the Commission determines additional certainty is appropriate,

Respondent recommends requiring that any option remain exercisable through the projected energization

date, not that the option be eliminated as an acceptable instrument altogether.


 III.​ THE NON-REFUNDABILITY OF FINANCIAL SECURITY AT THE PRE-STUDY STAGE

                   WILL BE FATAL TO LARGE LOAD DEVELOPMENT IN TEXAS


        Staff’s Proposal for Publication requires, under §25.194(d)(10), that a large load customer post

financial security of $100,000 per MW of requested peak demand at the time the intermediate agreement

is executed, that is, before ERCOT initiates the interconnection study.           Under §25.194(e), the

interconnecting DSP or TSP must coordinate with ERCOT to initiate the interconnection study within 60

days after execution of the intermediate agreement. This means the customer’s full $100,000-per-MW

security obligation is due and posted before any study commences and before the customer receives any

indication of available transmission capacity, required system upgrades, interconnection costs, or the

energization timeline. For a 500 MW data center project, this is $50 million in security posted into an

informational vacuum.


        The consequences of this timing become clear when read together with the withdrawal provisions

in §25.194(g).    If the customer subsequently receives unfavorable study results, as a great many

customers will, given the current state of the ERCOT queue and transmission constraints across much of

the system, and elects to withdraw, §25.194(g)(2) first applies the customer’s security to any outstanding

amounts owed (i.e., documented costs incurred by the DSP/TSP). After this drawdown, §25.194(g)(3)

refunds only 20% of the remaining balance to the customer. The remaining 80% of the balance is

forfeited: under §25.194(g)(4), it “must be paid to the interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an

                                                                                                        5
 offset to the interconnecting TSP’s rate base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate

proceeding or comprehensive rate proceeding.”


        The practical effect of this structure is draconian. A developer that posts $50 million in security

before studies begin, receives study results showing that the site is unviable or prohibitively expensive,

and rationally elects to withdraw, recovers at most 20% of whatever remains after documented costs, and

forfeits the other 80% to the utility’s rate base. If the DSP/TSP’s documented costs are modest (as they

often are at early stages), the developer’s forfeiture approaches $40 million on a 500 MW project. This

forfeiture occurs despite the customer acting rationally and in good faith, precisely because the study

process exists: to determine whether the project is viable before irreversible capital commitments are

made.


        This is not a financial commitment tied to cost causation. The 80% forfeiture to the TSP’s rate

base bears no relationship to costs incurred by the DSP/TSP to serve the customer; those costs are already

captured by the draw-down under §25.194(g)(2). What remains after that drawdown is, by definition,

security in excess of any costs the customer caused. Directing 80% of that excess to the TSP’s rate base is

simply a direct wealth transfer from the developer to the utility’s other ratepayers, with no cost-causation

link whatsoever. It is, in substance, a penalty imposed on developers for exercising the rational option to

withdraw from a project that the interconnection study itself has revealed to be unviable. This proposed

language is an affront to every effort to attract business to this state and is openly hostile to large load

customers.


        PURA §37.0561(i) expressly contemplates that security provided under subsection (h)(1) shall be

“refunded, in whole or in part,” under specified circumstances, including when a customer withdraws its

request for all or a portion of the requested capacity. The Legislature’s inclusion of this refundability

provision demonstrates its intent that security serve as a queue-management mechanism, a tool to screen

speculative projects and ensure financial seriousness, not as a punitive forfeiture regime that penalizes

                                                                                                          6
 rational development decisions.      The proposed 80/20 forfeiture structure in §25.194(g)(3)–(4) is

fundamentally inconsistent with this statutory intent. A rule that requires a customer to forfeit 80% of its

security upon withdrawal, at a stage when the customer has received no study results and had no basis

upon which to evaluate the viability of the project, does not “support business development in this state”

as required by PURA §37.0561(b). Instead, it deters business development in Texas.


        The impact will be felt most acutely in the data center sector, where developers often evaluate

multiple sites simultaneously across multiple states and ISO/RTO jurisdictions and make go/no-go

decisions based on relative cost, timeline, and risk certainty. No comparable interconnection framework

in the United States imposes financial exposure of this magnitude at the pre-study stage, or directs

forfeited security to the interconnecting utility's rate base. While other ISOs have adopted progressively

at-risk deposits to deter speculative queue entries, the amounts at risk at comparable early stages are an

order of magnitude smaller, and forfeited amounts are applied to cover documented study costs or

underfunded network upgrades, not transferred to the utility's rate base as a windfall to other ratepayers.

If Texas is the only major market where a developer must accept an 80% forfeiture of outsized pre-study

security upon withdrawal, rational developers will allocate their capital to other jurisdictions. The result

will not be a cleaner interconnection queue; it will be an empty one.


        Respondent strongly recommends that Staff revise the proposed rule to provide for full

refundability of financial security posted under §25.194(d)(10) for any project that withdraws prior to

some reasonable timeline after ERCOT’s completion of the interconnection study under §25.194(e), or

alternatively, prior to execution of the interconnection agreement under §25.194(f). At the intermediate

agreement stage, the DSP/TSP should retain only the amount necessary to cover documented,

unrecoverable costs actually incurred, consistent with the approach taken for generation interconnection

deposits under 16 TAC §25.195(e)(1)(B).          If the Commission determines that some degree of

non-refundability is necessary at this stage to deter purely speculative applications, Respondent



                                                                                                          7
 recommends that the forfeiture be limited to transparent study fees, not 80% of $100,000 per MW, and

further, that any forfeited amount of this $100,000 per MW be applied to offset the documented costs of

the interconnection process, not directed to the TSP’s rate base.


    IV.​ THE APPLICATION OF FORFEITED SECURITY TO THE UTILITY RATE BASE IS

       INEQUITABLE TO LOAD CUSTOMERS AND CREATES PERVERSE DISINCENTIVES

                                   FOR INTERCONNECTING UTILITIES


        Beyond the forfeiture amount itself, the proposed destination of forfeited security under

§25.194(g)(4) and (h)(4), the interconnecting TSP’s rate base, presents a distinct and independently

objectionable problem. By directing forfeited security as a rate-base offset, the proposed rule creates a

subsidy that flows exclusively to other ratepayers and distorts incentives for both TSPs and load

customers, thereby undermining the efficient interconnection of large loads.


        The incentive distortion operates on two levels. First, from the perspective of the interconnecting

TSP, a rate base offset is not a benefit to the utility; it is a reduction in the TSP’s rate base, which directly

reduces the revenue requirement on which the TSP earns its authorized return. When forfeited security is

applied to offset rate base under §25.194(g)(4) or (h)(4), the TSP’s investable asset base shrinks, and with

it the TSP’s earnings. The economic consequence for TSPs is clear: the proposed framework creates a

disincentive to pursue cost-effective interconnections for the load customer. Where a customer’s direct

interconnection costs under §25.194(f)(9) and system upgrade costs under §25.194(f)(10) are well below

$100,000 per MW, a large gap exists between the posted security and the costs incurred. If that customer

withdraws, the excess security, which is substantial precisely because the interconnection is inexpensive,

flows to offset the TSP’s rate base, reducing the TSP’s return. TSPs are therefore economically motivated

to direct their finite planning and engineering resources toward sites where interconnection facility costs

approach the $100,000 per MW security level, even though many viable sites could be interconnected at




                                                                                                               8
 far lower cost. The proposed rule thus drives TSP resources toward higher-cost interconnections and

away from lower-cost ones, the exact opposite of efficient resource allocation.


        Second, from the load customer's perspective, the proposed framework eliminates any benefit of

pursuing a project with lower interconnection costs. Under the 80/20 forfeiture structure, a customer that

withdraws forfeits 80% of its remaining security regardless of whether the interconnection would have

cost $10,000 per MW or $90,000 per MW.             The customer who selects a site requiring minimal

transmission investment, a site where the gap between the $100,000 per MW security and the directly

caused costs is widest, forfeits the most capital upon withdrawal, because the excess over documented

costs is greatest. The customer who selects a site requiring extensive upgrades forfeits less because the

draw-down under §25.194(g)(2) consumes a larger share of the security before the 80/20 split applies.

The rule, therefore, provides no incentive for load customers to seek out cost-effective interconnection

sites and, perversely, penalizes them most severely for identifying sites that would be least burdensome to

the system.


        The combined effect of these two distortions is a framework in which the forfeited excess

security, capital contributed by the developer with no cost-causation link, flows as a subsidy exclusively

to non-large load other ratepayers. Neither the TSP nor the load customer benefits from cost-effective

interconnection under this structure. The TSP is incentivized to avoid low-cost interconnections that

would erode its rate base. The load customer is penalized most for pursuing them. And the only

beneficiary, other ratepayers, receives a subsidy that is funded entirely by a wealth transfer from

developers who had no obligation, under any cost-causation principle, to provide it. This outcome is

inequitable, economically irrational, and antithetical to the Legislature’s directive under PURA

§37.0561(b) to support business development while minimizing stranded costs.


        Respondent has consistently maintained throughout this proceeding that the appropriate

framework is to have the customer offset its directly assigned facilities through CIAC, as §25.194(f)(9)

                                                                                                         9
 provides, and to maintain refundable security in place for system upgrades under §25.194(f)(10). If a

customer withdraws, the DSP/TSP should retain only the amounts necessary to cover documented,

unrecoverable costs actually incurred in reliance on the interconnection request, equipment that cannot be

canceled, construction that has commenced, and services that have been initiated, consistent with

§25.194(g)(2)(A)–(D).     Any security in excess of the documented costs should be refunded to the

customer in full. No portion of a customer’s security should flow to the TSP’s rate base. The proposed

80/20 mechanism removes the link between cost and recovery, transforms a financial commitment

requirement into a ratepayer subsidy funded by developers, and introduces incentives that are opposed to

the efficient, cost-effective interconnection of large loads in ERCOT.


                                               V.​ CLOSING


        Respondent appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and commends the

Commission and Staff for their continued work on this important rulemaking. However, the three

provisions addressed herein present profound concerns. The forfeiture of 80% of $100,000 per MW in

pre-study security under §25.194(g)(3)–(4), when the customer has no study results upon which to

evaluate the project, is a punitive construct with no cost-causation basis. The application of that forfeited

security to the TSP’s rate base under §25.194(g)(4) and (h)(4) constitutes a direct subsidy from developers

to other ratepayers while simultaneously disincentivizing TSPs from pursuing cost-effective

interconnections and eliminating any benefit to load customers from selecting lower-cost sites. The

exclusion of purchase options from §25.194(d)(1) and (f)(1) contravenes PURA §37.0561(g)’s express

authorization of alternative legal interests and represents the most restrictive site control standard in any

interconnection framework in the United States.


        Each of these provisions independently represents a significant barrier to large load development;

taken together, they create a regulatory framework that is transparently hostile to large load customers and

irreconcilable with the Legislature’s directive under PURA §37.0561(b).

                                                                                                          10
         Texas has long been the premier destination for large-scale infrastructure investment precisely

because its regulatory and market frameworks have balanced reliability with economic opportunity. The

decisions made in this proceeding will determine whether Texas retains that distinction or cedes it to other

states that offer more rational risk allocation for developers. Respondent respectfully and strongly urges

Commission Staff to revise the proposed rule to address the concerns identified herein, and to adopt

interconnection standards that fulfill the Legislature’s directive under PURA §37.0561(b) to “support

business development in this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and

maintaining system reliability.”




                                                           Respectfully submitted,




                                                           ​
                                                           Schaper Energy Consulting, LLC
                                                           3006 Brazos St., Ste. 200
                                                           Houston, Texas 77006
                                                           andrew@schaperintl.com

forfeits the other 80% to the utility's rate base. If the DSP/TSP's documented costs are modest (as they

often are at early stages), the developer's forfeiture approaches $40 million on a 500 MW project. This

forfeiture occurs despite the customer acting rationally and in good faith, precisely because the study

process exists: to determine whether the project is viable before irreversible capital commitments are

niade.

         This is not a financial commitment tied to cost causation. The 80% forfeiture to the TSP's rate

base bears no relationship to costs incurred by the DSP/TSP to serve the customer; those costs are already

captured by the draw-down under §25.194(g)(2). What remains after that drawdown is, by definition,

security in excess of any costs the customer caused. Directing 80% ofthat excess to the TSP's rate base is

simply a direct wealth transfer from the developer to the utility's other ratepayers, with no cost-causation

link whatsoever. It is, in substance, a penalty imposed on developers for exercising the rational option to

withdraw from a project that the interconnection study itself has revealed to be unviable. This proposed

language is an affront to every effort to attract business to this state and is openly hostile to large load

customers.


         PURA §37.0561(i) expressly contemplates that security provided under subsection (h)(1) shall be

"refunded, in whole or in part," under specified circumstances, including when a customer withdraws its

request for all or a portion of the requested capacity. The Legislature's inclusion of this refundability

provision demonstrates its intent that security serve as a queue-management mechanism, a tool to screen

speculative projects and ensure financial seriousness, not as a punitive forfeiture regime that penalizes

                                                                                                           6
 rational development decisions.      The proposed 80/20 forfeiture structure in §25.194(g)(3)-(4) is

fundamentally inconsistent with this statutory intent. A rule that requires a customer to forfeit 80% of its

security upon withdrawal, at a stage when the customer has received no study results and had no basis

upon which to evaluate the viability of the project, does not "support business development in this state"

as required by PURA §37.0561(b). Instead, it deters business development in Texas.


        The impact will be felt most acutely in the data center sector, where developers often evaluate

multiple sites simultaneously across multiple states and ISO/RTO jurisdictions and make go/no-go

decisions based on relative cost, timeline, and risk certainty. No comparable interconnection framework

in the United States imposes financial exposure of this magnitude at the pre-study stage, or directs

forfeited security to the interconnecting utility's rate base. While other ISOs have adopted progressively

at-risk deposits to deter speculative queue entries, the amounts at risk at comparable early stages are all

order of magnitude smaller, and forfeited amounts are applied to cover documented study costs or

underfunded network upgrades, not transferred to the utility's rate base as a windfall to other ratepayers.

If Texas is the only major market where a developer must accept an 80% forfeiture of outsized pre-study

security upon withdrawal, rational developers will allocate their capital to other jurisdictions. The result

will not be a cleaner interconnection queue; it will be an empty one.


        Respondent strongly recommends that Staff revise the proposed rule to provide for full

refundability of financial security posted under §25.194(d)(10) for any project that withdraws prior to

some reasonable timeline after ERCOT's completion of the interconnection study under §25.194(e),or

alternatively, prior to execution of the interconnection agreement under §25.194(f). At the intermediate

agreement stage, the DSP/TSP should retain only the amount necessary to cover documented,

unrecoverable costs actually incurred, consistent with the approach taken for generation interconnection

deposits under 16 TAC §25.195(e)(1)(B).          If the Commission determines that some degree of

non-refundability is necessary at this stage to deter purely speculative applications, Respondent



                                                                                                           7
 recommends that the forfeiture be limited to transparent study fees, not 80% of $100,000 per MW, and

further, that any forfeited amount of this $100,000 per MW be applied to offset the documented costs of

the interconnection process, not directed to the TSP's rate base.


    IV. THE APPLICATION OF FORFEITED SECURITY TO THE UTILITY RATE BASE IS

       INEQUITABLE TO LOAD CUSTOMERS AND CREATES PERVERSE DISINCENTIVES

                                   FOR INTERCONNECTING UTILITIES


        Beyond the forfeiture amount itself, the proposed destination of forfeited security under

§25.194(g)(4) and (h)(4), the interconnecting TSP's rate base, presents a distinct and independently

objectionable problem. By directing forfeited security as a rate-base offset, the proposed rule creates a

subsidy that flows exclusively to other ratepayers and distorts incentives for both TSPs and load

customers, thereby undermining the efficient interconnection of large loads.


        The incentive distortion operates on two levels. First, from the perspective ofthe interconnecting

TSR a rate base offset is not a benefit to the utility; it is a reduction in the TSP's rate base, which directly

reduces the revenue requirement on which the TSP earns its authorized return. When forfeited security is

applied to offset rate base under §25.194(g)(4) or (h)(4), the TSP's investable asset base shrinks, and with

it the TSP's earnings. The economic consequence for TSPs is clear: the proposed framework creates a

disincentive to pursue cost-effective interconnections for the load customer. Where a customer's direct

interconnection costs under §25.194(f)(9) and system upgrade costs under §25.194(f)(10) are well below

$100,000 per MW, a large gap exists between the posted security and the costs incurred. Ifthat customer

withdraws, the excess security, which is substantial precisely because the interconnection is inexpensive,

flows to offset the TSP's rate base, reducing the TSP's return. TSPs are therefore economically motivated

to direct their finite planning and engineering resources toward sites where interconnection facility costs

approach the $100,000 per MW security level, even though many viable sites could be interconnected at




                                                                                                              8
 far lower cost. The proposed rule thus drives TSP resources toward higher-cost interconnections and

away from lower-cost ones, the exact opposite of efficient resource allocation.


        Second, from the load customer's perspective, the proposed framework eliminates any benefit of

pursuing a project with lower interconnection costs. Under the 80/20 forfeiture structure, a customer that

withdraws forfeits 80% of its remaining security regardless of whether the interconnection would have

cost $10,000 per MW or $90,000 per MW              The customer who selects a site requiring minimal

transmission investment, a site where the gap between the $100,000 per MW security and the directly

caused costs is widest, forfeits the most capital upon withdrawal, because the excess over documented

costs is greatest. The customer who selects a site requiring extensive upgrades forfeits less because the

draw-down under §25.194(g)(2) consumes a larger share of the security before the 80/20 split applies.

The rule, therefore, provides no incentive for load customers to seek out cost-effective interconnection

sites and, perversely, penalizes them most severely for identifying sites that would be least burdensome to

the system.


        The combined effect of these two distortions is a framework in which the forfeited excess

security, capital contributed by the developer with no cost-causation link, flows as a subsidy exclusively

to non-large load other ratepayers. Neither the TSP nor the load customer benefits from cost-effective

interconnection under this structure.   The TSP is incentivized to avoid low-cost interconnections that

would erode its rate base.    The load customer is penalized most for pursuing them.        And the only

beneficiary, other ratepayers, receives a subsidy that is funded entirely by a wealth transfer from

developers who had no obligation, under any cost-causation principle, to provide it. This outcome is

inequitable, economically irrational, and antithetical to the Legislature's directive under PURA

§37.0561(b) to support business development while minimizing stranded costs.


        Respondent has consistently maintained throughout this proceeding that the appropriate

framework is to have the customer offset its directly assigned facilities through CMC, as §25.194(f)(9)

                                                                                                          9
 provides, and to maintain refundable security in place for system upgrades under §25.194(f)(10). If a

customer withdraws, the DSP/TSP should retain only the amounts necessary to cover documented,

unrecoverable costs actually incurred in reliance on the interconnection request, equipment that cannot be

canceled, construction that has commenced, and services that have been initiated, consistent with

§25.194(g)(2)(A)-(D).    Any security in excess of the documented costs should be refunded to the

customer in full. No portion of a customer's security should flow to the TSP's rate base. The proposed

80/20 mechanism removes the link between cost and recovery, transforms a financial commitment

requirement into a ratepayer subsidy funded by developers, and introduces incentives that are opposed to

the efficient, cost-effective interconnection of large loads in ERCOT


                                               V. CLOSING


        Respondent appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and commends the

Commission and Staff for their continued work on this important rulemaking.             However, the three

provisions addressed herein present profound concerns. The forfeiture of 80% of $100,000 per MW in

pre-study security under §25.194(g)(3)-(4), when the customer has no study results upon which to

evaluate the project, is a punitive construct with no cost-causation basis. The application ofthat forfeited

security to the TSP's rate base under §25.194(g)(4) and (h)(4) constitutes a direct subsidy from developers

to   other ratepayers   while   simultaneously disincentivizing TSPs from pursuing cost-effective

interconnections and eliminating any benefit to load customers from selecting lower-cost sites.          The

exclusion of purchase options from §25.194(d)(1) and (f)(1) contravenes PURA §37.0561(g)'s express

authorization of alternative legal interests and represents the most restrictive site control standard in any

interconnection framework in the United States.


        Each of these provisions independently represents a significant barrier to large load development;

taken together, they create a regulatory framework that is transparently hostile to large load customers and

irreconcilable with the Legislature's directive under PURA §37.0561(b).
